title: Why Control Comes Before the Cut

scenes.visual: Deep slate background (#0F172A). Large luminous outline of a single schematic cell fills 70% of the frame height in cool grey-blue (#94A3B8), breathing gently. Crisp white title 'Why Control Comes Before the Cut' (size 38) settles cleanly in the upper centre with no subtitle.

scenes.tts: How can a cell stay ready to destroy itself within hours, yet never trigger that switch by mistake? Animal cells carry killer enzymes called caspases. They cut other proteins apart. Unlike a phosphate tag, no enzyme can rejoin a cut peptide bond.
scenes.caption: How can a cell stay ready to destroy itself within hours, yet never trigger that switch by mistake? Animal cells carry killer enzymes called caspases. They cut other proteins apart. Unlike a phosphate tag, no enzyme can rejoin a cut peptide bond.
scenes.visual: Camera eases into the schematic cell cytosol (deep slate #0F172A). On the left, a sleek schematic protein bar carries a glowing cyan phosphate dot that smoothly attaches and detaches with a looping arrow ('Reversible tag'). On the right, a vivid red (#EF4444) caspase shears a protein bar cleanly in two; the cut halves drift apart as a faint cross-out mark appears over any return arrow ('Permanent cut'). All labels size 30, white (#F8FAFC), max 3 words.
scenes.narration: How can a cell stay ready to destroy itself within hours, yet never trigger that switch by mistake? Animal cells carry killer enzymes called caspases. They cut other proteins apart. Unlike a phosphate tag, no enzyme can rejoin a cut peptide bond.

scenes.tts: A kinase adds a phosphate, and a phosphatase takes it right back off. A caspase cut is permanent. Once caspases start cutting, the cell cannot undo the damage. To act fast yet stay safe, every caspase is made ahead of time as an inactive precursor. Those stored precursors wait silently throughout the cytosol.

scenes.visual: The reversible phosphate panel fades smoothly so the cell interior fills the frame. Inside the cytosol, muted crimson-rose (#FB7185) and muted orange (#FDBA74) rounded precursor blocks drift gently with slow ambient motion, each wearing a crisp white lock icon and label 'Inactive precursors' (size 30). No molecular structures; schematic blocks only.

scenes.tts: Apoptotic caspases come in two designs. Initiator caspases, such as caspase eight, float as single inactive chains. Executioner caspases, such as caspase three, are already paired into dimers. Surprisingly, those pairs stay silent because an uncut linker locks each active site shut. Only a cut unlocks them to slice targets.
scenes.caption: Apoptotic caspases come in two designs. Initiator caspases, such as caspase-8, float as single inactive chains. Executioner caspases, such as caspase-3, are already paired into dimers. Surprisingly, those pairs stay silent because an uncut linker locks each active site shut. Only a cut unlocks them to slice targets.
scenes.visual: The drifting precursors sort smoothly into two zones inside the cell. Upper cytosol: single muted crimson-rose (#FB7185) teardrop blocks labelled 'Initiators (caspase-8)'. Lower cytosol: joined pairs of muted orange (#FDBA74) blocks bridged by a dark clamping bar labelled 'Executioners (caspase-3)' and 'Uncut linker' (size 28). A brief subtle pulse highlights the clamping bar holding the orange active notches closed while gentle drift continues.
scenes.narration: Apoptotic caspases come in two designs. Initiator caspases, such as caspase-8, float as single inactive chains. Executioner caspases, such as caspase-3, are already paired into dimers. Surprisingly, those pairs stay silent because an uncut linker locks each active site shut. Only a cut unlocks them to slice targets.

scenes.tts: That puts the key decision on the initiator chains. To switch on, two initiator chains must meet and pair up. In a healthy cell, those single chains drift far apart across the cytosol. Pause and think: why don't they pair up and fire on their own?
scenes.caption: That puts the key decision on the initiator chains. To switch on, two initiator chains must meet and pair up. In a healthy cell, those single chains drift far apart across the cytosol. Pause and think: why don't they pair up and fire on their own?
scenes.visual: The lower executioner dimers dim slightly while the upper cytosol expands to fill 65% of the frame. Six muted crimson-rose (#FB7185) initiator monomers drift lazily far apart across the wide cytosolic space. Two wander close briefly, hesitate, and drift away. At the top, a high-contrast question banner settles: 'Why don't floating initiators pair up on their own?' (size 32, white #F8FAFC).
scenes.narration: That puts the key decision on the initiator chains. To switch on, two initiator chains must meet and pair up. In a healthy cell, those single chains drift far apart across the cytosol. Pause and think: why don't they pair up and fire on their own?

scenes.visual: Hold the question banner 'Why don't floating initiators pair up on their own?' cleanly at top while the six sparse crimson-rose (#FB7185) initiator monomers continue slow ambient drift across the wide cytosol, showing plenty of empty space between them. A subtle horizontal progress bar along the bottom ticks smoothly across 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Because they are too dilute to hold together on their own. Random bumps separate before anything happens. To switch them on, the cell builds an assembly platform that packs copies side by side. Crowded together, the chains pair up and activate. So for initiators, the first step is a gathering, not a cut.

scenes.visual: Question banner clears. Two drifting crimson-rose (#FB7185) monomers bump and bounce gently apart. Then a glowing schematic docking rack ('Assembly platform', size 30) rises into view and pulls four monomers in side by side. As adjacent monomers press together into pairs, their colour transforms smoothly from muted rose (#FB7185) to vivid active red (#EF4444) with a crisp radial glow.
scenes.narration: Because they are too dilute to hold together on their own. Random bumps separate before anything happens. To switch them on, the cell builds an assembly platform that packs copies side by side. Crowded together, the chains pair up and activate. So for initiators, the first step is a gathering, not a cut.

scenes.tts: One way to build that platform starts outside the cell. A killer T cell presents a three-part signal called Fas ligand. It binds a surface death receptor named Fas and pulls several Fas receptors into a cluster. A two-ended bridge protein called Fadd docks onto those clustered receptor tails. Its other end grabs inactive caspase eight.

It binds a surface death receptor named Fas and pulls several Fas receptors into a cluster. A two-ended bridge protein called FADD docks onto those clustered receptor tails. Its other end grabs inactive caspase-8.
scenes.visual: Camera pans smoothly up to the cool grey-blue (#94A3B8) plasma membrane arching across the top third (same cell world). From above, a three-lobed violet (#A78BFA) 'Fas ligand' arrives and slides separated violet 'Fas' transmembrane rods together into a tight cluster. Beneath the membrane, cyan (#38BDF8) two-ended bridge blocks ('FADD') dock onto the clustered Fas tails, and their lower sockets pull in muted crimson-rose (#FB7185) 'Procaspase-8' monomers. Small corner tag reads 'Schematic' (size 24).
scenes.narration: One way to build that platform starts outside the cell. A killer T cell presents a three-part signal called Fas ligand. It binds a surface death receptor named Fas and pulls several Fas receptors into a cluster. A two-ended bridge protein called FADD docks onto those clustered receptor tails. scenes.tts: Receptor, bridge, and initiator together form one platform: the death-inducing signaling complex, or disc. Inside the disc, caspase eight chains sit side by side, pair up, and switch on. No kinase or second messenger is needed here. Active caspase eight then clips the linker on executioner dimers, unlocking them to cut.
scenes.caption: Receptor, bridge, and initiator together form one platform: the death-inducing signaling complex, or DISC. Inside the DISC, caspase-8 chains sit side by side, pair up, and switch on. No kinase or second messenger is needed here. Active caspase-8 then clips the linker on executioner dimers, unlocking them to cut.
scenes.visual: A clean bracket encircles clustered violet Fas, cyan FADD, and crimson procaspase-8 with label 'DISC' (size 32). The crowded procaspase-8 chains snap together in pairs and flare vivid red (#EF4444). They release downward toward the muted orange (#FDBA74) executioner dimers waiting below; a bright shear flash snaps each dark linker bar, transforming the orange dimers into vivid amber-red (#F97316) active cutters ('Active executioners').
scenes.narration: Receptor, bridge, and initiator together form one platform: the death-inducing signaling complex, or DISC. Inside the DISC, caspase-8 chains sit side by side, pair up, and switch on. No kinase or second messenger is needed here. Active caspase-8 then clips the linker on executioner dimers, unlocking them to cut.

scenes.tts: Unlocked executioners cut hundreds of structural proteins and free an enzyme that chops D N A. Unlike an injured necrotic cell that swells and bursts, an apoptotic cell shrinks into neat, membrane-wrapped parcels. Neighbours swallow those parcels, so usually no inflammation follows. Because cuts are permanent, gathering initiators on a platform holds the trigger.

scenes.visual: Camera pulls back to show the whole schematic cell transforming cleanly: active amber-red (#F97316) executioners dismantle internal beams as the cell shrinks smoothly and pinches into tidy grey-blue (#94A3B8) membrane-wrapped parcels ('Apoptosis: intact parcels'), one engulfed by a neighbouring cell outline. Briefly beside it on the left, a ghosted contrasting cell swells and bursts outward ('Necrosis: spill'), then fades, leaving the clean parcels pulsing softly.

scenes.visual: Clean deep slate (#0F172A) end card with a single crisp white sentence centred (size 36, no subtitle or secondary line): 'Caspase cuts cannot be undone, so assembly platforms control initiator activation.'
